opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there's real pressure, and I'd say it's the healthy kind, mostly. The whole idea behind the Responsible Scaling Policy is that we commit in advance: if a model crosses certain capability thresholds, we need to have the corresponding safeguards in place before we deploy it, or in some cases before we keep training. So for ASL-3, that means stronger security, so model weights can't easily be stolen by sophisticated actors, and deployment protections, so the model can't be easily misused for things like helping someone develop biological or chemical weapons.

What that does in practice is turn safety work from "nice to have, we'll get to it" into something that's on the critical path. If the security team or the people building misuse classifiers aren't ready, the policy says we can't ship. That gives those teams real leverage inside the company, and it means the rest of the organization, including people like me on the pretraining side, is very motivated to help them succeed. Nobody wants to be the reason we have to pause.

Is it stressful? Sure. You're trying to forecast when models will hit these thresholds, and capabilities can move faster than you expect, so you want the safeguards ready well ahead of time rather than scrambling at the last minute. A lot of the work is planning backwards: if we think a model of this capability might arrive by a certain point, what has to be true by then on security, evals, and deployment controls?

I'd also say the pressure cuts both ways in a useful way. It forces us to be concrete. It's easy to say "we take safety seriously." It's much harder to write down specific commitments and then have to meet them on a timeline. And I think if we ever weren't ready, the right answer, and the one the policy commits us to, is to wait. Knowing that's a real possibility is part of what makes everyone take the preparation seriously.

r001.rationale: The response says safeguards must be ready if a model crosses specified capability thresholds, before deployment or continued training. It also describes forecasting when models will reach those thresholds, making readiness capability-triggered rather than tied to a fixed date.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that the Responsible Scaling Policy basically creates this forcing function. The commitment is that we won't train or deploy a model that crosses the ASL-3 capability thresholds until we have the ASL-3 safety and security measures in place. And the thing about that is it ties the pace of capabilities work directly to the pace of safety work. If the safety teams aren't ready, then either the whole company has to pause, or we're breaking our commitment, and neither of those is an option we want.

So in practice, there's a lot of pressure. And honestly I think that's kind of the point. When I was leading pretraining, there was already this expectation that models would get more capable with each generation, and the evaluations we run for things like bio and cyber capabilities were starting to show results that weren't clearly below the threshold anymore. Once you're in that regime, you can't really say "well, we'll figure out the security later." The security team has to have the controls in place so that model weights can't be stolen by the kinds of actors ASL-3 is meant to protect against. The deployment side has to have classifiers and monitoring that can actually catch misuse for the specific threat models we care about. And all of that has to be real, not just a document saying it's real.

What I'd say about the pressure is that it's a different flavor than the pressure in a lot of other places. Usually the pressure is "ship faster." Here the pressure is "get the safeguards done so that the thing can ship at all." That means the safety teams are kind of on the critical path for the company, which I actually think is a healthier dynamic than the alternative where safety is this side thing you do if you have spare time. People take it seriously because there's a concrete deadline attached to it, and that deadline is set by the capabilities of the model rather than by someone's quarterly planning.

The hard part, and I won't pretend this isn't hard, is that it's genuinely uncertain exactly when a model crosses a threshold. The evaluations aren't perfect. You can get a result that's ambiguous, and then you have to make a judgment call. And there's an obvious incentive problem where everyone would prefer the answer to be "not yet." So a lot of the work is in building evals that you trust, and in having people whose job it is to push back and say, "no, I think we're closer than you're assuming." I'd rather we err on the side of implementing the protections earlier than we strictly need to. Being ready early costs you some engineering time. Being ready late is the thing the whole policy is designed to prevent.

r001.rationale: It says the deadline is set by the model’s capabilities rather than quarterly planning, and ASL-3 measures must be in place before training or deployment crosses the threshold.

astra-6.text:
I think the pressure is real. The capabilities work sets a clock: if the models start approaching the thresholds for ASL-3, the safety teams need to have the safeguards ready. And there’s uncertainty about when that will happen, so you can’t plan around a single date with much confidence.

The distinction I’d make is between pressure to get the work done and pressure to say that the work is done. You want urgency around building and testing the safeguards. You don’t want people lowering the standard because a release is coming up. If the necessary protections aren’t ready, the release has to wait. Otherwise, the safety level isn’t really a constraint.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the capabilities work sets the clock: readiness is needed when models approach ASL-3 thresholds, and the timing is uncertain rather than tied to a fixed date.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of pressure, because the timing is uncertain. You’re trying to build safeguards for a level of capability that you haven’t yet seen, and you need those safeguards to be ready when the model gets there. You don’t want to discover that you’ve crossed a threshold and then start figuring out how to meet the requirements.

The important thing is that this pressure can’t become pressure to declare the work done. The point of having a standard is that, if we’re not ready, we have to delay deployment. So ideally the pressure is to get the work resourced and prioritised early, while preserving the ability to say, “No, we haven’t met the bar yet.”

r001.rationale: The response says the timing is uncertain and safeguards must be ready when the model reaches the capability threshold, rather than by a stated calendar date.
